title: Freeman On The Land Wins Court Case... Despite His "Silly" Arguments - A Lawyer Explains
summary: Canadian defence lawyer walks through R v Duncan (2013): the court dismissed the freeman jurisdiction arguments but acquitted because the police failed to prove a lawful arrest.

verdicts.note: Unilateral fee schedules create no contract; no court has enforced one and some senders have been prosecuted.
Meads rejected a unilaterally imposed fines scheme, and even Freeman founder Menard conceded fee schedules are illegitimate.
Fee schedules that officials supposedly accept by silence are a form of the Three/Five Letters scheme, which courts treat as notoriously false.

verdicts.note: Professional conduct rules bar advancing frivolous arguments, which is why most pseudolaw litigants are self-represented.

verdicts.note: Meads v Meads is widely cited across Canada and other common-law courts as authority to dismiss such arguments summarily.

Meads has been cited in 198 Canadian decisions, endorsed by five Courts of Appeal and followed across the Commonwealth, sparing judges from answering arguments 'piecemeal'; but only 33.6% of later OPCA judgments cite it.
Meads was cited in about 90 Canadian OPCA judgments and courts dismiss strawman arguments as simply false, but discrete legal errors still get detailed reasoned rejections.
Canadian courts widely adopted Meads as the key anti-pseudolaw authority, but Meads itself is a systematic rebuttal, not a licence to dismiss without reasons.
Courts often dismiss quickly to save resources, but Meads is praised for a thorough, explicit rebuttal, and Australasian courts increasingly give substantive rebuttals.
